common_name: Bell's Seedling Chilean Pernettya (Self-Fertile Prickly Heath)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade; unlike most female selections of this dioecious species, Bell's Seedling carries perfect flowers and sets a heavy crop on its own.

directions: Bell's Seedling is a UK-raised, RHS Award of Garden Merit selection of Chilean pernettya notable for being a rare hermaphrodite form of an otherwise dioecious species, so it fruits reliably as a single plant rather than needing a separate male shrub nearby. It still sets an even heavier crop of berries when a male Gaultheria mucronata is grown within bee range, so gardeners assembling a mixed planting can pair it with a male selection for maximum yield. The berries are a bright, deep red and ripen in autumn, persisting on the low, needle-leaved evergreen mounds well into winter. Give it the same acidic, consistently moist, humus-rich woodland conditions as other ericaceous shrubs, and use it as a groundcover-scale edging plant beneath taller acid-loving shrubs.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Gaultheria mucronata 'Bell's Seedling' AGM plant profile
Burncoose Nurseries — Gaultheria mucronata cultivar notes

common_name: Mulberry Wine Chilean Pernettya (Dark Magenta-Fruited Prickly Heath)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade; this is a female selection and needs a male Gaultheria mucronata growing nearby to set its berries.

directions: Mulberry Wine is a female Chilean pernettya cultivar grown for its unusually large, rounded berries that ripen from pink through a deep wine-red to purple, giving the plant its name. Because the species is dioecious, a male seedling or male-flowered cultivar must be planted within pollinator range for Mulberry Wine to set its showy fruit each autumn. The low, mounding evergreen habit and small, glossy, needle-like leaves make it a useful acid-soil groundcover or edging shrub in a woodland border, where the fruit persists into winter after the foliage of nearby perennials has died back. Grow it exactly as other ericaceous shrubs — moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in dappled shade, with a thick organic mulch to keep roots cool and evenly moist through summer.
sources: Burncoose Nurseries — Gaultheria mucronata 'Mulberry Wine' cultivar profile
Shoot Gardening — Gaultheria mucronata 'Mulberry Wine' plant guide

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade; this is a female selection and needs a male Gaultheria mucronata growing nearby to set its berries.

directions: Wintertime is a female Chilean pernettya selection grown for its pure white berries, a striking contrast to the pinks, reds, and purples of most other Gaultheria mucronata cultivars, and it holds an RHS Award of Garden Merit for garden performance. As a female clone of a dioecious species it needs a male G. mucronata planted nearby to pollinate its flowers, but once fertilized the berries are notably long-persisting, often holding their color and firmness on the plant well past midwinter. The dense, low, prickly-leaved evergreen mound works well as underplanting beneath rhododendrons, camellias, or other acid-loving shrubs, where its winter fruit display stands out against darker foliage. Provide the same moist, humus-rich, lime-free soil and part-shade woodland conditions required by the species.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Gaultheria mucronata 'Wintertime' plant profile
Burncoose Nurseries — Gaultheria mucronata cultivar notes

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 4-6 feet apart in rows at least 8 feet apart, and set up a two- or three-wire trellis since the semi-erect canes benefit from support once heavily loaded with fruit.

directions: Twilight is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry released by the USDA-ARS breeding program in cooperation with Oregon State University, selected from a cross of the thornless 'Ouachita' with a thornless USDA breeding selection. It ripens relatively early for a semi-erect type and is valued for large, very firm berries with tough skin and a distinctively crisp texture that holds up well to shipping. Canes are vigorous and largely self-supporting, though a simple trellis keeps heavily laden fruiting laterals off the ground and makes harvest easier. Cut fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest each year and tie in the current season's primocanes, which will carry next year's crop.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — 'New Blackberries: Eclipse, Galaxy, and Twilight' research news
US Plant Patent PP30879 — Blackberry plant named 'Twilight'

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 4-6 feet apart in rows at least 8 feet apart, and set up a two- or three-wire trellis since the semi-erect canes benefit from support once heavily loaded with fruit.

directions: Eclipse is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry released by the USDA-ARS breeding program with Oregon State University, notable along with its sibling release 'Galaxy' for being among the first cultivars to combine germplasm from both the eastern and western North American blackberry breeding pools. It produces uniformly shaped, medium-sized berries on vigorous, largely self-supporting canes. A simple trellis is still worthwhile to keep fruiting laterals upright and organized for picking, especially in a home planting where rows are short. As with other floricane-fruiting blackberries, remove spent canes to the ground immediately after harvest and train the new season's primocanes in their place for next year's crop.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — 'New Blackberries: Eclipse, Galaxy, and Twilight' research news
HortScience — 'Eclipse' Thornless Semi-erect Blackberry cultivar description

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 4-6 feet apart in rows at least 8 feet apart, and set up a two- or three-wire trellis since the semi-erect canes benefit from support once heavily loaded with fruit.

directions: Galaxy is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry from the USDA-ARS breeding program in Corvallis, Oregon, bred from a cross of the unpatented selection 'ORUS 1393-1' with the thornless 'Triple Crown'. Its medium-large, dark, firm berries ripen early within the semi-erect fruiting season, and like its sibling release 'Eclipse' it draws on both eastern and western North American blackberry germplasm for improved vigor and fruit quality. Canes are largely self-supporting but produce heavier, more manageable harvests when tied to a simple two-wire trellis. Remove fruited floricanes at ground level right after harvest and train in the new primocanes to bear the following season's crop.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — 'Galaxy' thornless semierect blackberry publication
US Plant Patent Application — Blackberry plant named 'Galaxy'

common_name: Black Pearl Blackberry (Thornless Trailing Processing Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 6-8 feet apart in rows at least 8-10 feet apart, and install a sturdy multi-wire trellis since the long trailing canes will not support themselves.

directions: Black Pearl is a thornless, trailing blackberry released by the USDA-ARS breeding program with Oregon State University, one of three thornless trailing cultivars (alongside 'Black Diamond' and 'Nightfall') developed to give the processing industry machine-harvestable alternatives to the thorny standard 'Marion'. Trials found its fruit quality, once frozen and processed, comparable to Marion, making it attractive for jam, juice, and bakery use in addition to fresh eating. Train the long, sprawling canes onto a sturdy multi-wire trellis, since like other trailing blackberries they need full support and generous row spacing. Cut fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest and tie in the current season's primocanes for next year's crop, and site the planting for excellent air movement to limit fungal disease in humid climates.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — 'Black Pearl' Thornless Trailing Blackberry, HortScience 2005
Oregon State University Extension — Caneberry Production Guide

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 6-8 feet apart in rows at least 8-10 feet apart, and install a sturdy multi-wire trellis since the long trailing canes will not support themselves.

directions: Nightfall is a thornless, trailing blackberry released by the USDA-ARS breeding program with Oregon State University alongside two sibling releases, 'Black Diamond' and 'Black Pearl', as part of an effort to give growers machine-harvestable, thornless alternatives to the thorny industry-standard 'Marion'. Like its siblings it produces firm, dark fruit suited to both fresh use and commercial processing. The long trailing canes need a sturdy multi-wire trellis and generous spacing to manage their sprawling growth, so fan-train fruiting canes along the wires each season. Remove spent floricanes to the ground right after harvest and tie in the new primocanes, and give the planting full sun with excellent air circulation to reduce disease pressure in humid climates.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — 'Nightfall' Thornless Trailing Blackberry, HortScience 2005
Oregon State University Extension — Caneberry Production Guide

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 6-8 feet apart in rows at least 8-10 feet apart, and install a sturdy multi-wire trellis since the long trailing canes will not support themselves.

directions: Metolius is a trailing blackberry from the USDA-ARS breeding program in Corvallis, Oregon, prized as one of the earliest-ripening trailing cultivars available, well ahead of older Pacific Northwest standards. Breeders selected it for fruit firm enough to hold up to wholesale fresh-market shipping, a trait uncommon among the earliest-ripening trailing types, and it has been evaluated for cold hardiness and machine-harvest suitability in Pacific Northwest trials. The long, sprawling canes need a sturdy multi-wire trellis and generous row spacing to manage their trailing growth. Cut fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest and train in the season's new primocanes, and provide full sun with good air movement, since trailing blackberries bred for the cool, dry Pacific Northwest can be more disease-prone in hot, humid climates.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — 'Metolius' Trailing Blackberry cultivar publication
Oregon State University Extension — Caneberry Production Guide

common_name: Wild Treasure Blackberry (Thornless Wild-Flavor Trailing Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 6-8 feet apart in rows at least 8-10 feet apart, and install a sturdy multi-wire trellis since the long trailing canes will not support themselves.

directions: Wild Treasure is a thornless trailing blackberry released in 2010 by the USDA-ARS breeding program, bred from a cross between a selection of the wild Pacific dewberry (Rubus ursinus) and the thornless trailing cultivar 'Waldo'. It was specifically developed to recapture the small, intensely flavored, wild-blackberry character of native R. ursinus in a plant that is thornless and machine-harvestable, unlike the prickly wild species itself. The long, trailing canes need a sturdy multi-wire trellis and wide row spacing typical of trailing types. Cut fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest, tie in the new primocanes for next year's crop, and favor a cool-summer, well-drained, full-sun site, since trailing blackberries of this parentage are best suited to Pacific Northwest-like growing conditions.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — 'Wild Treasure' Thornless Trailing Blackberry, HortScience 2010
Oregon State University Extension — Caneberry Production Guide
